name: Jade Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the Clinicbook office on Mill Street by half eight, before the open-plan room gets loud. We make booking and billing software for dental clinics, about 60 of us, and I lead the billing side. Most of my day is reading code, fixing the bugs clinics phone in about, and reviewing what the three developers under me wrote. I love the quiet hour before standup, our short morning team meeting, when it's just me and a hard problem.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The constant push to use AI tools, honestly. Management keeps sending links about coding assistants, the programs that write code for you, and I keep not clicking. I don't trust code I didn't reason through myself, and in billing a rounding mistake means a dentist charges a patient twice. Then there's money: I have a master's degree, I lead a team, and I still have less than a month's rent put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At work I'd point out that the coding assistants made a lot of noise and we still need people who understand the billing rules line by line. Online I'd share a long article about the hype and add one sarcastic sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, but it doesn't fix my real problem, which is that I'm underpaid and stuck. Clinicbook knows there are maybe four software firms in Dunmore, so they don't have to pay me what I'd get in a big city. Even with AI fizzling, I'm one bad month away from borrowing from my mum, and she cleans offices for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it and push for a proper pay review in the spring, with figures from salary surveys. I'd try to put 150 a month aside, which sounds tiny but would be my first real savings since the master's. And I'd keep pushing the idea of a staff association at Clinicbook, because nobody negotiates well alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired relief. The AI fear goes away, but the old knot in my stomach about rent stays exactly where it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a staff association. How would that go down at Clinicbook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. Our founder, Martin, likes to call us a family, and families don't organise, apparently. But half the support team is on short contracts, and if a senior like me says it out loud, the juniors might feel safer joining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if a month went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The student loan comes straight out of my pay, so really it would be food and the phone. I'd drop the phone contract and live on the office wifi. I've done it before, the winter my mum's cleaning hours got cut.

say: I'd say the **coding assistants** were mostly noise and careful people still matter.
I'd post a long article about the **hype** with one dry line of my own.
think: The plateau is a **relief**, but my real problem is being underpaid with nowhere else to go.
Clinicbook pays below city rates because there are only about **four software firms** in Dunmore.
One bad month and I'd be **borrowing from Mum**, who cleans offices.
do: Push for a **pay review** in spring, armed with salary survey figures.
Save **150 a month**, my first real savings since the master's.
Keep building support for a **staff association** among the juniors.
feel: **Tired relief** that the AI fear has gone.
The old **knot** about rent and bills stays put.
S0.quote: Even with AI fizzling, I'm one bad month away from borrowing from my mum, and she cleans offices for a living.
fieldNote: Her job feels **safe**, but money worry was there long before AI came up.
She frames her low pay as a **local trap**: she stayed in Dunmore for her mother.
Even with nothing changing, she reaches for **collective** answers before personal ones.

steps.text: Keep leading Clinicbook's billing code and ask for a spring pay review
Ask the junior developers to back a Clinicbook staff association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice companies are making, not the weather. Coding is right there on the list, and if Clinicbook uses AI to stop hiring juniors, that's a decision to save money on people. I'd post that the gains should go into shorter weeks or better pay, not just the founder's margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in trouble, and it's partly my own stubbornness. If Martin says every developer uses the assistant or goes, I either give in or I'm out, and there's nowhere else in Dunmore to go. Being the best at billing only protects me as long as my bosses think billing needs a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd write down every billing rule that lives in my head, so the company has to treat that knowledge as worth paying for. I'd join the national tech workers' union this month instead of waiting for Clinicbook to have one. And I'd cancel the gym and the takeaways so I could save something before the first round of cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cornered. Angry at the company, and a bit angry at myself for never even trying the tools once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd document the billing rules. Doesn't that make it easier to replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that scares me. But if I don't, the knowledge walks out with me and the clinics send wrong bills, and that's patients paying for my pride. I'd rather be the one who wrote the rulebook than the one who hid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, the junior I hired last year. He's brilliant but slow and careful, which is exactly what a manager with an AI tool stops valuing. If cuts start at the bottom, he's the first name on the list, and he sends money home every month.

say: I'd say job cuts from AI are a **company choice**, not bad luck.
I'd argue the savings should fund **shorter weeks** or better pay for staff.
think: I'm **in trouble**, partly because I've refused to touch the tools.
If the assistant becomes **compulsory**, I give in or leave, with no other local employer.
My skill only protects me while managers believe **billing needs a human**.
do: Write up every **billing rule** in my head for the team.
Join the national **tech workers' union** this month.
Cancel the **gym and takeaways** to save before any cuts.
feel: A bit **angry at myself** for never trying the tools.
S1.quote: Being the best at billing only protects me as long as my bosses think billing needs a human.
fieldNote: She admits her **refusal** to use AI is part of her risk, without changing it.
Writing down the billing rules is about **patients**, not just job security.
Her first worry for others goes to **Kofi**, a junior who supports family.

steps.text: Write every Clinicbook billing rule into the team wiki
Join the national tech workers' union this month
Cancel the gym membership and stop takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this needs to be stopped or slowed by law, and I'd mean it. A technology that replaces most office work in two years with no plan is a social emergency. I'd say that at work, in every group chat, and at whatever protest there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't have a plan, and two years is less time than my student loan has left. My whole job is thinking work at a screen, so I'm in the 2028 wave, not the robot wave. Everything I'd fall back on, like teaching coding or tech support, is thinking work too, so it goes at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for work that needs hands, because that has until about 2031. My uncle Samir runs a small kitchen-fitting business, and I'd ask if he'd take a 27-year-old apprentice who's good with measurements. And I'd give up the flat and move back in with my mum to stop the rent draining away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, if I'm honest. I spent six years training to stand on a floor that disappears in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning let you do that you couldn't do otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, with less than a month saved. Two years is enough to see it coming but not enough to retrain properly and save up, not on what Clinicbook pays. Maybe enough to learn to fit a kitchen badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years after. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the hands-on job I'd scramble into is on a timer too, just a slower one. I'd start again at the bottom in 2028 and maybe lose that by 2031. That's what makes it panic and not just fear: no step is safe for long.

say: I'd call for a **legal pause** or slowdown and say so everywhere.
I'd call AGI in two years a **social emergency** and turn up to protests.
think: I have **no plan**, and two years is shorter than my loan.
My job is pure **screen work**, so it goes in 2028, not 2031.
Every fallback I know, like **teaching coding**, goes at the same time.
do: Ask my **uncle Samir** about an apprenticeship fitting kitchens.
Give up the flat and **move back** in with Mum.
Join any **protest** pushing for a legal slowdown.
feel: **Panic**, like the floor I trained six years for is going.
S2.quote: I spent six years training to stand on a floor that disappears in two years.
fieldNote: With **thin savings**, two years of warning buys her almost nothing.
She sees the robot gap as a **second timer**, not as a refuge.
Her actions are scrambles, not a plan; she says so **herself**.

steps.text: Join protests calling for a legal slowdown on AGI
Ask Uncle Samir for a kitchen-fitting apprenticeship
Give up the flat and move back in with Mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd say the same thing, louder and with more organisation behind it. I'd want my union pushing for a law that makes companies pay into retraining for every job they automate. I'd say it at work too, even if Martin rolled his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the difference between falling off a cliff and climbing down one. If I moved home now, I could save for the first time and train for something before 2031 instead of after. The awful bit is that I'd probably still end up in hands-on work that robots reach in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move back to my mum's within six months and put the rent, around 600 a month, straight into savings. I'd take a part-time electrical course in the evenings at Dunmore college. And I'd stay at Clinicbook as long as they'd have me, because the pay still beats anything else in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but less wild about it. More like watching a storm come over the hills than being caught out in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools at work in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, grudgingly, near the end, if it kept the job another year. But I'd rather spend my learning time on wiring than on teaching a machine to do my job faster. That probably sounds stubborn; it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya, your flatmate, about leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya the truth: I'm going home because I'm scared and it's the sensible thing. She works at the library, and I'd tell her to think about her own job too, because cataloguing is thinking work. Then we'd argue about who keeps the kettle.

say: I'd push my union for a **retraining levy** on firms that automate.
I'd say it at work too, even if the **founder** rolled his eyes.
think: Five years turns a **fall** into a climb down.
Moving home would let me **save** and train before 2031.
I'd still likely land in hands-on work that **robots** reach by 2034.
do: Move back to Mum's within **six months** and bank the rent.
Take an **evening electrical course** at Dunmore college.
Stay at Clinicbook **as long as possible** for the pay.
feel: **Frightened**, but steadier than in the two-year picture.
Like watching a **storm** come rather than being caught in it.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between falling off a cliff and climbing down one.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her **scramble** into a sequence: move, save, train.
She would rather learn **wiring** than AI tools, and owns the stubbornness.
She still expects to **lose the job**, so the fear stays high.

steps.text: Move back to Mum's house within six months
Bank the 600 a month saved on rent
Take an evening electrical course at Dunmore college
Push the union to campaign for a retraining levy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently if governments actually use it. Shorter working weeks, retraining paid for by the companies that profit, a proper safety net. I'd say that's the minimum, and I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. By 2036 I'd be 37, with a trade and some savings, and still most of a working life ahead. I'd still lose the job I trained for, but I wouldn't lose my footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Clinicbook for the next few years and really push for that pay rise, because I'd need the money to change paths. Around year four, once I had a few months saved, I'd start an electrician's apprenticeship. I'd keep the union card and vote for whoever puts a retraining fund in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad for the work I love, and calmer about my own life. Still a knot, just a looser one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you never use the tools. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. With ten years I might try them in year two or three, just to understand what's coming for us. I'd still write the billing code myself; I just wouldn't pretend the tools don't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the people you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what stops me feeling fine. Kofi and the other two would have to do what I'm doing, with even less money. I'd try to get Clinicbook to pay for evening courses as part of any change, and I'd want it in writing.

say: I'd say ten years is enough **if governments act** on it.
I'd call for **shorter weeks**, company-paid retraining and a safety net.
think: Ten years feels **survivable**; I'd be 37 with a trade.
I'd lose the career I trained for but **keep my footing**.
do: Stay at Clinicbook and push hard for a **pay rise**.
Start an **electrician's apprenticeship** around year four.
Vote for whoever writes down a **retraining fund**.
feel: **Sad** for the work she loves, but calmer about her life.
S4.quote: I'd still lose the job I trained for, but I wouldn't lose my footing.
fieldNote: Ten years is the first picture where she describes a **real plan**.
She softens on AI tools only to **understand the threat**, not to use them.
Her worry shifts to her **team**, who have even less money to change paths.

steps.text: Stay at Clinicbook and press for a pay rise
Start an electrician's apprenticeship around year four
Vote for parties promising a company-funded retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have no money, no time and nothing safe to step onto. What would help is a law that gives workers a year's pay and a paid training place when their job is automated, paid for by the companies doing it. That, and a union at Clinicbook that already exists before the day comes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why someone who's good at this is paid so little. It's because I stayed in Dunmore for my mum, and companies know people like me can't leave. People who can't move are the ones AI will squeeze hardest, and nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: People who can't move are the ones AI will squeeze hardest, and nobody talks about that.
portrait: Jade, 27, leads billing code at **Clinicbook**, a 60-person dental software firm in Dunmore.
She has a master's but **under a month** saved, and stays local for her mother.
She has **never used AI tools** and trusts only code she has reasoned through.
She reaches for **unions and laws** first, and blames company choices, not technology.
Her fear climbs from uneasy to **panic** at two years, easing as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no money, no time and no safe job to step onto.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving automated workers **a year's pay** and a paid training place.
A **union at Clinicbook** that exists before the cuts arrive.
